summary: Fixes earlier specifications that used underscored DNS node names before a registry existed. Now that RFC 8552 defines the registry, this document updates those specifications so they register and use their names correctly. It is a Best Current Practice.

eli5.summary: Before there was a shared list for special folder names, different groups picked names on their own. This document tidies up the old rules so they match the new list.

questions: which rfcs use underscored dns labels
what is an underscored dns node name
what is the underscored and globally scoped dns node names registry
subtitle: Updates dozens of older specifications so their underscored DNS names fit into the single IANA registry created by RFC 8552.

tldr.problem: Many specifications picked underscored DNS node names such as _tcp before any registry existed, so the names came from one shared namespace with no coordination.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8552 created one IANA registry for these names. This RFC marks the older specifications as updated, gives templates for registering TXT, SRV and URI names, and rewrites the SRV, URI and DNSSEC signaling texts.
tldr.outcome: The changes keep existing software and operational practice working while bringing the old specifications in line with the registry model. The RFC introduces no new IANA registries or procedures.

facts.label: Registry
facts.value: Underscored and Globally Scoped DNS Node Names

today: RFC 8553 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 222). The unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC, and it updates many earlier RFCs, from RFC 2782 to RFC 8145.

sections.title: Why Old Specifications Need Fixing
sections.content:
Early uses of an underscore as the start of a DNS node name were defined without any IANA registry. The underscore creates a space for constrained interpretation of resource records, but the result was an entirely uncoordinated set of name-creation activities all drawing from the same namespace. RFC 8552 now defines a registry, the "Underscored and Globally Scoped DNS Node Names" registry.

The registry model is that each entry is unique by the combination of a resource record type and a global (highest-level) underscored node name, meaning the underscored name closest to the DNS root.

The existing specifications do not mention this registry, so a new reader or editor gets no signal that the names are processed through IANA. This document fixes that by marking each published document with an update. It also revises the SRV and URI specifications, which provide a meta-template for underscored names partly based on separate registries. The result preserves existing software and operations practice.
sections.eli5: Many groups invented their own special names with no shared list. This document points all those old rules at the new shared list.

sections.title: Underscored Names Scope a Record Type
sections.content:
The use of underscored node names is specific to each resource record (RR) type being scoped. An underscored name defines a place in the DNS tree. It does not define the rules for what appears below that place, whether more underscored names or a leaf node holding records. Those rules come from the specification for each RR type.

The RFC then looks at three RR types: TXT, SRV and URI. For each it describes how existing specifications use underscored names, and how the global underscored name should be registered.
sections.eli5: A special folder name marks a spot in the address book. The rules for what goes inside that spot are written elsewhere, by whoever owns that kind of record.

sections.title: Registration Templates for TXT, SRV and URI
sections.content:
For each of the three record types, the RFC gives a generic approach that serves both as an update to existing specifications and as guidance when those documents are revised. For any document that uses the type under an underscored name, the global node name is expected to be registered in the IANA registry. An effort was made to find existing documents, register their global names and list them in the registry's initial set.

For future specifications, the RFC supplies suggested text for the IANA Considerations section, beginning "Per RFC 8552, please add the following entry". The entry has an RR Type column, a node name column and a reference column.

  • TXT: the node name is the underscored DNS node name. Documents listed include RFC 5518, RFC 5617, RFC 6120, RFC 6376, RFC 6763, RFC 7208 and RFC 7489.
  • SRV: the global name is the 'protocol' name, following the SRV template in RFC 2782. Many documents fall in this category, such as RFC 3263 and RFC 5389.
  • URI: the global name is either the 'protocol' name or the highest-level Enumservice name, following RFC 7553.
sections.eli5: The document gives fill-in-the-blank forms. A group that wants a special name fills in the form, and the name goes on the shared list.

sections.title: Text Changes to SRV, URI and DNSSEC Signaling
sections.content:
The RFC gives exact OLD and NEW text for three specifications, and each also gets a normative reference to RFC 8552.

SRV (RFC 2782). The SRV format is _Service._Proto.Name TTL Class SRV Priority Weight Port Target, with DNS type code 33. The new text says the Proto name is the symbolic protocol name with an underscore prepended to prevent collisions with DNS labels that occur in nature, and that _TCP and _UDP are at present the most useful values. It drops the old wording that allowed any name defined by Assigned Numbers or locally. It adds that the global 'protocol' underscored name SHOULD be registered in the IANA registry.

URI (RFC 7553). Section 4.1 gets the same SHOULD for the global name. Valid service parameters are split into two kinds: those in the "Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry" and those in the Enumservice registrations. The Enumservice parameters are reversed, prefixed with an underscore and prepended as separate labels, and the highest-level Enumservice name becomes the global name to register. For example, an ENUM service parameter "A:B:C" for example.com is queried as _C._B._A.example.com with type URI.

DNSSEC signaling (RFC 8145). That RFC uses node names starting with _ta- when querying the NULL RR. The new text says an entry is registered in the IANA registry for all node names beginning with _ta- under the NULL RR.
sections.eli5: The document shows the old sentence and the new sentence side by side, so editors can see exactly what changed and why.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: The RFC refers to IANA registries but introduces no new registries or procedures. The registry and its rules come from RFC 8552. This document only changes how older specifications point at it.
sections.eli5: No new lists are made here. The document only points old rules at the list that already exists.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says only that this memo raises no security issues. It is a set of editorial and registry-alignment changes that preserve existing software and operational practice, so it adds no new protocol behavior.
sections.eli5: Nothing new happens here that could be unsafe. It is just tidying of old rules.
